items.title: What Is a Digital Product Passport? How Scanning a QR Code Changes Everyday Shopping
items.summary: If you have bought a jacket, pair of sneakers, or electronic device recently, you have probably noticed standard QR codes printed on wash tags or box packaging. Soon, those codes will do far more than link to a brand's home page. Under new European Union…
items.content_html:
If you have bought a jacket, pair of sneakers, or electronic device recently, you have probably noticed standard QR codes printed on wash tags or box packaging. Soon, those codes will do far more than link to a brand's home page.

Under new European Union regulations, millions of everyday products sold across Europe are receiving a Digital Product Passport (DPP).

To businesses and logistics workers, DPPs require industrial scanners and database integrations. But for everyday consumers, the concept is far simpler: your smartphone is the scanner, and a quick scan reveals the true story behind what you are buying.

Here is what Digital Product Passports mean for consumers, what information they unlock, and how they are changing the way we shop, repair, and recycle.

1. How It Works: Your Smartphone Is the Scanner

You do not need to buy specialized hardware or download heavy third-party apps to access a Digital Product Passport.

Every product equipped with a DPP carries an optical tag—usually a standard QR code or GS1 DataMatrix code—printed on its physical label, care tag, or outer casing.

When you open your smartphone’s camera app and point it at the code:
  1. Your phone reads the unique web link embedded in the tag.
  2. Your browser opens a verified web page linked directly to the product’s official digital file.
  3. The passport displays accurate, regulated data about that specific item.

2. What Information Can You Actually See?

Unlike traditional marketing tags that show glossy promotional ads, the data inside an official DPP is regulated by law. It cuts through "greenwashing" to give shoppers clear, verifiable facts.

When you scan a product passport, you typically unlock five key details:

Verified Sustainability & Carbon Footprint

Instead of vague claims like "sustainably sourced," the passport provides hard data on the item's total carbon footprint, water consumption during manufacturing, and raw material origins.

Real Material Composition

Want to know if a sweater is actually 100% organic cotton or a blend of synthetic polyester? The passport lists every material, organic certification, and whether recycled content was used. It also highlights any hazardous substances or microplastics present.

Repair Guides & Spare Part Ordering

Over 75% of European consumers say they would prefer to repair damaged goods rather than replace them. Scanning a product’s DPP opens official repair manuals, troubleshooting steps, and direct links to order compatible spare parts—helping keep appliances, electronics, and clothing out of landfills.

Proof of Authenticity & Ownership

For high-value goods, luxury fashion, or electronics, the passport acts as a digital certificate of authenticity. It helps protect buyers against counterfeit goods when buying secondhand.

End-of-Life Recycling Instructions

When a product reaches the end of its usable life, scanning the tag shows exact instructions on how to safely dispose of or recycle the item, including where to take old batteries or textiles.

3. When Will You See DPP Codes in Stores?

Digital Product Passports are being rolled out progressively across different industries:
  • Industrial & Electric Vehicle Batteries: Mandatory starting in February 2027.
  • Textiles, Apparel & Footwear: Phasing in throughout 2027.
  • Electronics, Furniture & Appliances: Following between 2027 and 2029.
  •  
By the end of the decade, scanning a product passport before buying will be as commonplace as checking an ingredient list on food packaging.

4. What This Means for Everyday Life

The shift toward Digital Product Passports gives power back to consumers.

Rather than relying on brand advertising, anyone with a smartphone can instantly verify whether a brand lives up to its ethical and environmental promises. It makes fixing broken items simpler, buying secondhand goods safer, and choosing durable products easier than ever before.

items.title: In-Store, Warehouse, or Customs: Identifying Your Scanning Workflow
items.summary: Selecting the right Digital Product Passport (DPP) scanner technology isn't just about reading a 2D code—it is about matching hardware and software capability to specific entry points in the product lifecycle. A scanner designed for receiving thousands of boxed goods at a distribution center port…
items.content_html:
Selecting the right Digital Product Passport (DPP) scanner technology isn't just about reading a 2D code—it is about matching hardware and software capability to specific entry points in the product lifecycle.

A scanner designed for receiving thousands of boxed goods at a distribution center port will fail to deliver the aesthetic, quick-checkout experience needed at a luxury fashion retail store. Conversely, a retail point-of-sale scanner cannot handle the rugged, high-speed demands of an automated recycling facility.

This guide maps out the four primary operational workflows where DPP scanning occurs, detailing the exact technical setup required for each environment.

1. Retail & Point of Sale (POS): Consumer & Staff Interactions

In a retail setting, DPP scanning serves a dual purpose: processing transactions at checkout and enabling customer engagement on the sales floor.

Operational Setup

  • Primary Objective: Seamless checkout speed, anti-counterfeit verification, and public product transparency.
  • Scanning Entities: Store staff, inventory clerks, and consumers.

Recommended Hardware & Software Configuration

  • Staff & POS: Omnidirectional 2D presentation scanners at cash wraps, or compact handheld wireless imagers. Devices must instantly process GS1 Digital Link codes to pull item price and serial data into the POS system.
  • Customer BYOD (Bring Your Own Device): Clear, highly visible 2D codes printed on hangtags or care labels that customers scan using standard smartphone camera apps to open the brand’s public DPP web interface.

2. Warehousing & Logistics: Batch Processing & Inbound/Outbound Flow

In distribution centers, freight forwarding hubs, and supply chain bottlenecks, efficiency is measured in units processed per minute. Manual single-item scanning often creates severe operational delays.

Operational Setup

  • Primary Objective: Rapid inbound receiving, automated sorting, high-volume outbound dispatch, and batch verification.
  • Scanning Entities: Warehouse operators, forklift drivers, automated conveyor systems.

Recommended Hardware & Software Configuration

  • Conveyor Arrays: Overhead multi-camera vision systems mounted above conveyor lines to read 2D codes on moving packages without stopping the line.
  • RFID Portals: Loading dock arches that read hundreds of UHF RFID passport tags simultaneously as palletized goods pass through warehouse doors.
  • Long-Range Handhelds: Wireless 2D imagers with laser guidance, allowing forklift operators to scan pallet tags on high racks from up to 15 meters away without leaving the cab.

3. Customs & Market Surveillance: Inspection & Compliance Verification

At EU border checkpoints and national market surveillance facilities, regulatory officials must verify that imported goods meet environmental, chemical, and ethical guidelines before entering the European market.

Operational Setup

  • Primary Objective: Verifying passport authenticity, validating EU Central Registry records, and enforcing import restrictions.
  • Scanning Entities: Customs officers, trade inspectors, market surveillance authorities.

Recommended Hardware & Software Configuration

  • Rugged Enterprise Handhelds: IP67-rated mobile Android terminals equipped with high-performance optical engines capable of reading worn, wet, or dirty codes on shipping containers and crates.
  • Authenticated Verification Apps: Mobile software integrated with official EU government authentication layers (EN 18239/18246 standards), allowing officers to instantly unlock restricted compliance certificates and test lab reports unavailable to the public.

4. Recycling & End-of-Life Processing: Material Recovery & Sorting

At the end of a product's lifecycle, recycling plants, refurbishers, and scrap processors use the DPP to extract critical information about material composition, hazardous substances, and dismantling steps.

Operational Setup

  • Primary Objective: Identifying recyclable materials (e.g., precious metals, specific polymers), locating hazardous chemicals (e.g., in industrial batteries), and accessing disassembly guides.
  • Scanning Entities: Sorting technicians, automated robotic sorters, industrial recyclers.

Recommended Hardware & Software Configuration

  • Direct Part Mark (DPM) Readers: Specialized industrial scanners equipped with polarized and multi-angle lighting engines to read laser-etched matrix codes on worn, dirty, or heat-damaged parts.
  • Automated Industrial Vision Systems: High-resolution cameras linked to optical sorting machinery that read passport data in real-time to trigger pneumatic air-jets or robotic arms for material separation.
  • ERP/WMS Integration Middleware: Software that feeds scanned material composition data directly into industrial processing databases.

Workflow Comparison Matrix

Workflow Environment Primary Operator Scan Speed Requirement Key Hardware Crucial Software Capability
Retail / POS Cashiers, Consumers High (Sub-second) 2D Presentation Imagers, Smartphone BYOD POS integration, consumer web rendering
Logistics & Warehousing Warehouse Staff, Automated Lines Very High (Batch/Continuous) Conveyor Vision Arrays, RFID Portals WMS API integration, batch processing
Customs & Inspection Government Authorities Medium (Detailed Audit) Rugged Mobile Terminals (IP67) Secure government API, role-based access
Recycling & End-of-Life Industrial Technicians, Automated Systems High (Sorting Speed) DPM Industrial Imagers, Vision Systems Material breakdown parsing, ERP routing

Key Takeaway for Business Operations

Before investing in equipment, map out every point where a product will be scanned throughout its lifecycle. A complete DPP strategy usually requires a hybrid model: open optical codes (like QR/GS1 DataMatrix) for retail and public access, combined with long-range or automated readers (like RFID or conveyor vision arrays) for backend logistics and recycling.

items.title: GS1 Digital Link & Interoperability: How DPP Scanners Talk to the EU Registry
items.summary: For IT directors and system integrators, the primary challenge of European Union Digital Product Passport (DPP) compliance isn't the physical scanner—it's the data payload behind the scan. A scanner that reads a barcode without knowing where to send the request or how to authenticate the…
items.content_html:
For IT directors and system integrators, the primary challenge of European Union Digital Product Passport (DPP) compliance isn't the physical scanner—it's the data payload behind the scan.

A scanner that reads a barcode without knowing where to send the request or how to authenticate the user is just a expensive laser pointer. To build a compliant system, technical leaders must understand GS1 Digital Link and the open interoperability standards that connect physical products to European data registries.

The Core Standard: What Is GS1 Digital Link?

Traditionally, standard 1D barcodes (EAN/UPC) contain only a static Global Trade Item Number (GTIN) that identifies a product category at checkout.

The EU DPP framework relies on GS1 Digital Link (standardized under ISO/IEC 18219 / EN 18219). GS1 Digital Link embeds web architecture into standard 2D data carriers like QR codes and GS1 DataMatrix symbols.

Instead of returning a simple sequence of numbers, scanning a GS1 Digital Link outputs a web-standard URI structured like this:

[https://id.brand.com/01/04012345678901/21/SER12345](https://id.brand.com/01/04012345678901/21/SER12345)

  • [https://id.brand.com](https://id.brand.com): The domain hosting the company's DPP resolver software.
  • /01/04012345678901: The Application Identifier (01) representing the GTIN (Global Trade Item Number).
  • /21/SER12345: The Application Identifier (21) representing a unique, item-level serial number.
This structure bridges the physical world and the web: it functions as a standard web link for smartphone cameras while acting as a structured, machine-readable data string for enterprise ERP and WMS scanners.

The 4-Step Lifecycle of a DPP Scan

When an operator or consumer scans a DPP tag, a precise sequence of technical steps occurs within milliseconds behind the scenes:
  1. Data Capture & Extraction: The physical scanner reads the optical code or NFC tag and passes the raw GS1 Digital Link URI string to the device software or middleware.
  2. Domain Resolution: The scanner's software queries the resolver server indicated in the URI.
  3. Registry Lookup via Open APIs: The resolver identifies the specific product and queries the decentralized brand database or the EU Central Registry using standardized EN 18220 / EN 18222 API protocols.
  4. Payload Delivery: The system returns JSON-LD formatted data containing the verified product passport attributes.

Role-Based Access Control: One Code, Multiple Views

A single product carries only one physical DPP code. However, different stakeholders requiring access to the passport have fundamentally different data needs and legal authorization levels.

Under European standards (including EN 18239 and EN 18246 security protocols), the scanning middleware must inspect the credentials of the scanning entity before serving the response payload.

                    ┌─────────────────────────┐
                    │ Physical DPP 2D Carrier │
                    └────────────┬────────────┘
                                 │
                         [ GS1 Scan Event ]
                                 │
                  ┌──────────────┴──────────────┐
                  ▼                             ▼
         Unauthenticated Scan          Authenticated Scan
        (Public / Consumer)          (Customs / Recycler)
                  │                             │
                  ▼                             ▼
         ┌───────────────────┐        ┌───────────────────┐
         │ Public Web Portal │        │  Restricted Data  │
         │ - Carbon Footprint│        │ - Chemical Sheet  │
         │ - Care & Repair   │        │ - Dismantling     │
         │ - Origin / Certs  │        │ - Import Status   │
         └───────────────────┘        └───────────────────┘
  • Consumers (Unauthenticated): Scanning with a standard smartphone camera redirects to a consumer-facing web page showing environmental impact scores, sustainability origin, care guides, and material composition.
  • Recyclers & Repair Centers (Authenticated): Scanning with certified industry software authenticates the user, unlocking technical dismantling instructions, hazardous material locations, and component spare-part identifiers.
  • Customs & Market Surveillance (Government Authenticated): Scanning via secure EU verification tools provides real-time validation of import compliance, testing certifications, and supply chain origin proofs.

Avoiding Vendor Lock-In: The Open API Architecture

When evaluating scanning software and middleware, the single biggest risk is adopting proprietary, closed-loop ecosystems. If a vendor uses proprietary URL structures or closed data formats, your scanning hardware will fail when communicating with external supply chain partners or state regulators.

Architectural Requirements for Technical Compliance

Layer Industry Requirement Why It Matters
Data Carrier ISO/IEC 18219 (GS1 Digital Link) Universal readability across public smartphones and industrial readers
Data Format JSON-LD / W3C Verifiable Credentials Machine-readable, standardized linked data formats readable by any system
API Layer EN 18220 / EN 18222 standards Seamless interoperability between brand systems and EU Central Registry gateways
Security Layer EN 18239 / EN 18246 Encrypted authentication for role-based access to restricted technical data

Key Takeaways for IT Integration

  1. Hardware Must Output Raw Strings: Ensure your optical scanners pass raw, unmanipulated URI strings to your software layer rather than stripping domain prefixes.
  2. Verify Resolver Flexibility: Choose software middleware that allows you to point your GS1 Digital Links to alternative resolvers should your cloud hosting or regulatory providers change.
  3. Prioritize JSON-LD Support: Your WMS, ERP, and scanning software must be capable of parsing JSON-LD payloads natively to ingest product passport data directly into business workflows.

items.title: Choosing the Right Scanner for Your Industry
items.summary: With EU Digital Product Passport (DPP) regulations phasing in—starting with industrial and EV batteries in February 2027, followed by textiles, apparel, and electronics—procurement and operations teams face a critical choice: which physical scanning hardware actually fits our operational workflow? A scanner that works perfectly at…
items.content_html:
With EU Digital Product Passport (DPP) regulations phasing in—starting with industrial and EV batteries in February 2027, followed by textiles, apparel, and electronics—procurement and operations teams face a critical choice: which physical scanning hardware actually fits our operational workflow?

A scanner that works perfectly at a clean retail checkout counter will fail instantly in an oil-slicked battery recycling plant or on a high-speed garment conveyor line. Choosing the wrong hardware leads to scanned-read errors, workflow bottlenecks, and high replacement costs.

This buyer’s guide breaks down the physical hardware requirements across four key industry sectors to help you make a confident, future-proof procurement decision.

1. Textiles & Apparel: High-Speed & Variable Data Carriers

The textile industry faces unique physical challenges. Data carriers (QR codes or GS1 DataMatrix symbols) are often printed on flexible wash labels, embroidered into fabrics, or laser-printed on swing tags. Over time, labels get crumpled, washed, faded, or creased.

Primary Hardware Options

  • Handheld 2D Area Imagers (High-Density Optics): Look for scanners equipped with high-density (HD) optical engines designed to capture small or damaged 2D symbols on soft, uneven surfaces.
  • Retail POS 2D Presentation Scanners: In-store checkout environments require hands-free, omnidirectional imagers capable of reading codes at any angle, including off customer smartphone screens or worn care tags.

Key Features to Prioritize

  • Motion Tolerance: Fast reading capability when workers are rapidly scanning garments during sorting or checkout.
  • Crumpled/Damaged Code Decoding: Built-in image reconstruction software to read wrinkled or washed-out fabric tags.
  • Light Weight & Ergonomics: High daily scan volumes require lightweight handhelds (under 200 grams) to prevent operator fatigue.

2. Industrial & Automotive Batteries: Heavy Duty & Direct Part Markings (DPM)

Under Regulation (EU) 2023/1542, electric vehicle, light transport, and industrial batteries above 2 kWh placed on the EU market must carry a battery passport. Because paper labels do not survive harsh chemical or thermal environments, data identifiers are usually etched directly into metal casings, ceramic headers, or battery modules.

Primary Hardware Options

  • Direct Part Mark (DPM) Industrial Handhelds: Scanners built specifically with specialized multi-angle LED lighting (diffuse, direct, and polarized light) to eliminate reflection on shiny metallic surfaces and read laser-etched matrix codes.
  • Heavy-Duty Rugged Terminals (IP67 Rated): Portable Android enterprise devices wrapped in rubberized housing, built to survive 2-meter drops onto concrete floors and chemical exposure.
  • Industrial RFID / NFC Readers: High-power handheld or fixed RFID portals to query internal battery management systems (BMS) or external NFC tags without requiring direct line-of-sight.

Key Features to Prioritize

  • Advanced Lighting Modes: Ability to switch between diffuse illumination for reflective metals and dark-field illumination for low-contrast laser scratches.
  • Ingress Protection (IP65/IP67): Sealed against industrial dust, moisture, and chemical splashes.
  • High Temperature Tolerance: Operational reliability in non-climate-controlled factory and recycling environments.

3. Consumer Electronics & High-Value Goods: Micro-Codes & High Security

Laptops, smartphones, home appliances, and power tools carry minute components with tight spatial constraints. Data carriers here are frequently micro-QR codes or tiny high-density DataMatrix symbols measuring under 3mm x 3mm.

Primary Hardware Options

  • High-Resolution Handheld Imagers: Scanners featuring 1280x800 pixel or higher sensors specifically calibrated for close-range micro-code reading.
  • Integrated Fixed-Mount Cameras: Stationed above quality-assurance and repair benches to automatically scan component passports as electronics pass along assembly lines.

Key Features to Prioritize

  • Macro Focal Length: Scanners capable of focusing as close as 1 to 2 centimeters from tiny circuit board codes.
  • Bluetooth 5.0 Wireless Range: Cordless mobility around large workbench environments with zero latency.
  • Integrated Secure Secure Elements: Encryption chipsets inside wireless scanners to prevent data interception during high-value product registration.

4. Logistics, Warehousing & Port Freight: Long-Range & Batch Reading

In distribution centers, freight forwarding hubs, and customs checkpoints, efficiency is determined by speed and range. Workers cannot afford to climb pallets or dismount forklifts to scan individual product boxes.

Primary Hardware Options

  • Extended-Range 2D Imagers: Scanners utilizing auto-focus laser guidance capable of reading a standard 2D barcode from 15 centimeters out to 20 meters away.
  • Fixed Conveyor Vision Systems: Multi-camera overhead arrays mounted above conveyor belts that capture and process GS1 Digital Link codes on moving boxes without stopping line flow.
  • UHF RFID Portal Gates: Automated frames installed at warehouse loading docks that read hundreds of item-level RFID passport chips simultaneously as a pallet passes through.

Key Features to Prioritize

  • Extended Read Ranges: Auto-focus engines that seamlessly transition between near-field item tags and high-rack pallet codes.
  • Battery Longevity: Hot-swappable, high-capacity batteries (4000+ mAh) guaranteed to last full 12-hour shifts.
  • 5G & Wi-Fi 6E Connectivity: High-bandwidth wireless interfaces to ensure immediate data transmission to warehouse management systems (WMS).

Quick Comparison: Hardware Specs by Sector

Industry Sector Primary Data Carrier Key Hardware Type Essential Specs
Textiles & Apparel QR Code, GS1 DataMatrix Handheld / POS Imagers High-density optics, motion tolerance, lightweight design
Batteries & Automotive DPM (Laser-Etched), Industrial NFC DPM Industrial Readers Polarized lighting, IP67 dust/water rating, drop resistance
Consumer Electronics Micro-QR, Ultra-dense DataMatrix Macro-Focus Imagers Megapixel sensor, close-range focus, secure wireless encryption
Logistics & Customs GS1 Digital Link, UHF RFID Extended-Range / RFID Gates 20m read distance, hot-swap battery, Wi-Fi 6E / 5G

Procurement Checklist: 5 Questions Before Placing an Order

  1. What is the smallest code physical size we will encounter? (Ensures you buy standard range vs. high-density or macro optics).
  2. What surface is the code printed or etched on? (Determines if you need specialized lighting for reflective metals or direct part markings).
  3. What IP rating does our environment demand? (Ensures devices survive dust, drops, moisture, or extreme temperature shifts).
  4. How far away will the operator be from the tag? (Distinguishes between contact desktop scanners and long-range extended imagers).
  5. Will the device interface directly with handheld mobile OS or legacy POS systems? (Confirms driver support for iOS, Android Enterprise, Windows, or Linux).

items.title: What is a "digital product passport scanner"? hardware vs. software explained
items.summary: One of the most common early questions when implementing European Union Digital Product Passport (DPP) compliance is "What kind of scanner do we need to buy?". A DPP scanner is not a single physical device like the barcode reader at a grocery store checkout. Instead,…
items.content_html:
One of the most common early questions when implementing European Union Digital Product Passport (DPP) compliance is "What kind of scanner do we need to buy?".

A DPP scanner is not a single physical device like the barcode reader at a grocery store checkout. Instead, it is an integrated ecosystem made up of two distinct parts: physical data capture hardware and digital resolution software.

Understanding how these two components work together is essential to making smart procurement decisions, avoiding redundant hardware purchases, and ensuring your operational workflows comply with EU standards.

The Hardware Layer: Capturing the Data Carrier

The physical hardware is responsible for one job: reading the optical tag or wireless signal attached to a product and converting it into a digital string (typically a standardized URL).

Depending on your industry, product type, and operating environment, the hardware layer usually falls into one of four categories:
  • 2D Optical Image Scanners: Standard 1D laser scanners cannot read the high-density data required for DPPs. You need 2D area imagers capable of reading QR codes, micro-QR codes, and GS1 DataMatrix codes. These can be handheld devices, fixed overhead mountings above conveyor belts, or desktop readers.
  • Direct Part Marking (DPM) Readers: In industries like industrial equipment or batteries, physical labels can wear away or burn off. DPM readers use specialized lighting and high-resolution sensors to read data matrices laser-etched directly onto metal, plastic, or ceramic surfaces.
  • RFID and NFC Readers: For high-volume logistics, apparel, or high-value goods, Near Field Communication (NFC) or Ultra-High Frequency (UHF) RFID tags are common. Scanners here are radio receivers—either handheld units or automated portal arches that read hundreds of items per second as pallets pass through a warehouse door.
  • Smartphones and Mobile Terminals: For retail staff, customs inspectors, or field service technicians, standard smartphones or rugged Android enterprise handhelds equipped with high-performance camera engines frequently serve as the physical hardware.

The Software Layer: Resolving and Unlocking Data

Capturing the code is only 10% of the job. Scanning a DPP data carrier typically yields a web address formatted as a GS1 Digital Link (for example: [https://dpp.brand.com/01/01234567890128/21/ABC12345](https://dpp.brand.com/01/01234567890128/21/ABC12345)).

Without software, scanning that code simply opens a standard webpage—or worse, returns a raw string of unreadable data. The software layer (often called a DPP Resolver or Middleware) turns that raw scan into actionable business intelligence.

The software handles three core tasks:
  1. Data Resolution: The software takes the product ID from the scan and queries the relevant registry or company database to pull the official product passport file.
  2. Role-Based Access Control (RBAC): Not everyone should see the same information. When a consumer scans a garment, the software displays public data: carbon footprint, material composition, and care instructions. When a recycling facility or customs inspector scans the exact same code with authenticated software, the system unlocks restricted data: chemical breakdowns, disassembly guides, or import clearance documentation.
  3. System Integration: The scanning software pushes structured data directly into your existing Enterprise Resource Planning (ERP), Warehouse Management System (WMS), or Point of Sale (POS) software.

Hardware vs. Software: Where Should You Spend Your Budget?

When allocating budget for DPP readiness, leadership teams often overspend on specialized hardware while neglecting software integration.

Category Hardware Focus Software Focus
Primary Function Reading physical tags accurately Processing, verifying, and routing passport data
Key Metric Scan speed, durability, light tolerance API response time, security standards compliance
Implementation Risk Buying equipment that cannot read small/etched tags Buying proprietary software locked to a single vendor
Cost Driver Per-unit device hardware costs Integration fees and platform licensing
Your organization may already own hardware capable of reading 2D codes or RFID tags. The gap may be the middleware required to authenticate scans against EU compliance standards and parse role-restricted data.

Evaluating Your Requirements

Before committing to hardware or software contracts, ask your technical and operations teams three questions:
  1. Where will scans take place? (In a dusty factory floor, a retail counter, a port authority checkpoint, or a recycling yard?)
  2. Who is doing the scanning? (Automated machinery, company employees using enterprise software, or external third parties using open mobile browsers?)
  3. What systems need to receive the data? (Does the scan just need to show a visual report on screen, or must it automatically trigger inventory updates in your WMS?)
By separating physical capture from digital processing, you can select hardware built for your specific physical environment while deploying software flexible enough to adapt as EU regulations evolve over the coming years.
